tier_reason: First-party README claim backed by a public harness (examples/perf_test/perf_test.py), the raw CSVs and plotting script (examples/perf_test/output/*.csv, compare.py) and a named board (Raspberry Pi 3B+, Ubuntu 20.04 64-bit). It falls short of A because only 'GCC -O3' is given: no compiler version, and the build command for the committed libalpha-lib-aarch64*.so binaries, including whether OpenMP was on, is not documented.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: up to 3.5x faster than the same routine without NEON intrinsics for small images, and around 1.4x for very large images. From the committed CSVs (examples/perf_test/output, derived from page data): for square images of 1-200 px per side, 0.93x at 1 px (NEON slower), 1.40x at 33 px, 2.53x at 97 px and 3.47x at 200 px, with a maximum of 3.58x at 186 px; for 50-5000 px, 1.37-1.40x from 450 to 1650 px, rising to 1.54-1.59x from 2450 to 5000 px.
corrections.workload: overlay_alpha_stride (div255_round) on random square BGRA images, sides 1-200 px in steps of 1 (small) and 50-5000 px in 100 steps (large), called through Python ctypes by examples/perf_test/perf_test.py. Time per call is averaged over max_size*10/size iterations, one run per size. The NEON build is compared with the same library built with DISABLE_NEON (scalar fallback with GCC unroll/ivdep pragmas, left to GCC -O3 auto-vectorization).
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the library's own non-NEON fallback (overlay_alpha_1 looped 8x under '#pragma GCC unroll 8' and 'ivdep'), not an external incumbent such as OpenCV. GCC version unstated, and the gain depends on how well that version auto-vectorizes the fallback. Timing runs from Python via ctypes, and both paths use '#pragma omp parallel for', so a fixed per-call overhead of about 20 us deflates the ratios below about 30 px (NEON is 0.93x at 1 px). It is not documented whether the committed .so files were built with OpenMP. Each size was run once with no variance reported. Raw data is public in examples/perf_test/output, and the prebuilt aarch64 and x86_64 .so files are committed.

notes: README claim matches the committed CSVs: 3.58x max on small images, and 1.4x at mid sizes rising to about 1.55-1.59x at the largest sizes, so 'around 1.4x' slightly understates the largest images. Metadata checked: GPL-3.0, 23 stars, not a fork, last commit 2020-07-26 (abandoned). Shortcomings: self-baseline (own scalar fallback), GCC version unstated, ctypes/OpenMP call overhead in the timing, single run per size.

tier_reason: First-party 'Possible results' sample in the README, with no CPU model, compiler version or flags. The harness is public (benchmarks/despacebenchmark.c, built with -march=native by CMakeLists.txt) and compares against the repo's own scalar loops, so the evidence is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README sample ('Possible results', unnamed CPU), in cycles per byte: despace (scalar) 5.337891, faster_despace 1.689453 and despace64 2.429688, against sse4_despace_branchless_u4 0.351562 (15.2x vs despace and 4.8x vs faster_despace, derived from page data) and avx2_despace_branchless_u2 0.535156 (10.0x vs despace and 3.2x vs faster_despace, derived from page data); memcpy reference 0.111328.
corrections.workload: Removing ' ', '\n' and '\r' in place from an 8 KiB buffer (N=8192) of random bytes above 32 with about 3% whitespace (1% of each character). Best of 100 repetitions, with the output length checked. The README sample reports cycles per byte; the current harness prints GB/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README sample; the README notes clang gives better results than gcc. The current CMakeLists.txt builds the library and benchmarks/despacebenchmark.c with -march=native (GCC or clang, x86-64 only). The README build line sets -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, but the Makefile's build and 'make benchmark' targets configure without a build type, so a single-config generator build gets no -O level.
corrections.caveats: The README output is labelled 'Possible results': a sample on an unnamed CPU, in the cycles/op format of an older harness. The current benchmarks/despacebenchmark.c prints GB/s and warns that its estimates are 'for illustrative purposes and may not be accurate'. The 15x headline is against the naive branchy despace loop; against the repo's best scalar version (faster_despace, a table-driven branchless loop) the SIMD gain is about 3-5x (derived from page data). A single 8 KiB in-cache buffer with 3% whitespace is used, so other densities were not tested. The Makefile path builds without optimization flags. The linked 2017 blog post was not opened (blogs blocked).

notes: All README numbers match the record. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 159 stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-09-05 (stale). Shortcomings: unnamed CPU, no flags or compiler version, sample output from an older harness, headline ratio against the naive loop rather than the best scalar loop (about 4.8x), and 'make benchmark' configures without a build type.

tier_reason: First-party README table (best of 50, cycles/byte) on a '2.4GHz Haswell laptop', with no CPU model or compiler version. The harness is a private modification of the fastvalidate-utf-8 benchmark and is not in the repo, so the evidence is C. The numbers also predate the 2019-11-17 correctness fix (2b0ad07), which would cap them at C regardless.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table, cycles per byte, best of 50: on 64K random UTF-8, z_validate_utf8_avx2 0.264 vs validate_utf8_fast_avx 0.410 and validate_utf8_fast_avx_asciipath 0.436 (1.55x and 1.65x, derived from page data); on 16M UTF-8, 0.290 vs 0.496 and 0.457 (1.71x and 1.58x, derived from page data). The README text says roughly 1.5-1.7x faster than fastvalidate-utf-8. On random ASCII there is no gain over the asciipath variant: 0.079 vs 0.074 (64K) and 0.160 vs 0.156 (16M). The SSE4 version (0.568 on 64K UTF-8) is slower than the AVX2 baseline.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark run, whose harness (a modified fastvalidate-utf-8 benchmark) is not published. The repo's rules.py builds the library with cc -O3 -march=native -std=gnu11 -DAVX2 or -DSSE4 (plus -fcolor-diagnostics, a clang flag); compiler version unstated.
corrections.caveats: The license is MIT, given only in the header of z_validate.c (commit 507bdea 'Add MIT license to library'). There is no LICENSE file, and test.lua and rules.py carry no license text. The baseline is an older SIMD validator, not a scalar one, and the 'fastest validator in the world' statement is the author's. The benchmark harness is a private modification and is not in the repo. The README table was written on 2019-11-15, before the error tables were fixed for missing F0 overlong sequences on 2019-11-17 (2b0ad07, a correctness bug reported on HN) and before the ASCII early-exit change on 2019-11-18 (cf48201), so the numbers were measured on pre-fix code. The baseline fastvalidate-utf-8 is marked obsolete in its own README in favour of simdutf (already catalogued). Only AVX2 and SSE4 are supported, and AVX-512 is untested.

notes: Numbers match the README table. The license was wrong in the record: z_validate.c carries an MIT header, so usability is copyable. Metadata checked: 222 stars, 8 commits, not a fork, last commit 2019-11-18 (abandoned). Shortcomings: private harness, unnamed CPU model and compiler, numbers predating a correctness fix (F0 overlong), no ASCII gain over the asciipath baseline, and a baseline that is itself superseded by simdutf.
